A close reading for the week

“There is an ecstasy that marks the summit of life”

The Call of the Wild · Chapter III

A stolen house-dog runs a rabbit down through the moonlit snow, and London stops the story to say what the running means: that the highest moment of being alive is the one in which you forget you are alive at all.

All that stirring of old instincts which at stated periods drives men out from the sounding cities … the blood lust, the joy to kill1—all this was Buck’s, only it was infinitely more intimate. He was ranging at the head of the pack, running the wild thing down, the living meat, to kill with his own teeth.2

  1. 1

    The joy of the kill

    London names it flatly: “the blood lust, the joy to kill”. The novel treats Buck’s descent into predation as an ascent to be celebrated, where another book would mourn a fall. Killing is presented as joy, and the prose wants the reader to feel it as joy. The book disturbs and thrills for the same reason: it is an adventure story from the children’s shelf whose moral centre is the ecstasy of taking life.

  2. 2

    “With his own teeth”

    London contrasts modern men who kill “by chemically propelled leaden pellets” (guns, from a distance) with Buck killing “the living meat” directly, “with his own teeth”. The animal’s violence is more “intimate” and, in the book’s logic, more honest than the sportsman’s. Buck does not hide behind technology from what killing is. The passage prefers the wolf to the hunter.
